issues.legal_issue: A revisional authority may not reassess facts as an appellate body, and a writ court may set aside a revision order that reverses supported findings without identifying a permissible defect.
material_facts: The Settlement Officer found the holdings to be joint family property after considering historical property documents, joint accounts, family arrangements, revenue payments, and other evidence.

The Deputy Director reached a different factual conclusion but did not identify that the Settlement Officer’s findings were perverse, unsupported by evidence, contrary to law, or affected by a root-level procedural irregularity.
The High Court quashed the Deputy Director’s order because it had improperly considered the evidence and had failed to account for evidence considered by the Settlement Officer.
issues.conclusion: The Deputy Director could not disturb the Settlement Officer’s findings merely by reaching a different view of the facts, and the High Court was justified in quashing the Deputy Director’s order.
issues.legal_principle: Under amended Section 48 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, revisional powers extend to examining the regularity, correctness, legality, and propriety of an order, but do not equate to appellate powers or permit a de novo factual assessment. Interference is permissible where findings are perverse, unsupported by or against the weight of evidence, contrary to law, or affected by a material procedural irregularity. The Court relied on Ram Dular v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, Seshmani v. Deputy Director of Consolidation, and Sheo Nand v. Deputy Director of Consolidation. The High Court’s exercise of jurisdiction under Article 226 to quash the defective revision order was upheld.

rule.if: consolidation_revision and subordinate_finding_supported_by_evidence and revisional_authority_reweighed_facts and no_permissible_defect_identified and writ_challenge_to_revision_order

predicates.consolidation_revision: The proceeding is a revision concerning findings made by authorities in a consolidation matter.
predicates.subordinate_finding_supported_by_evidenc: The subordinate authority reached its factual finding after considering evidence in the record.
predicates.revisional_authority_reweighed_facts: The revisional authority reached a different factual view by reassessing the evidence.
predicates.no_permissible_defect_identified: The revisional authority did not identify that the subordinate finding was unsupported, perverse, contrary to law, or affected by a material procedural irregularity.
predicates.writ_challenge_to_revision_order: A party challenged the revisional authority’s order in a writ proceeding.

issues.definition: When a consolidation revision merely replaces an evidence-supported factual finding with a different view, without identifying a permissible defect, the revisional authority cannot reverse that finding and a writ court may quash its order.

issues.legal_issue: Members of a continuing joint Hindu family may collectively hold tenancy property even though the family itself is not a juristic person and the tenancy rights devolve under the governing tenancy legislation.
material_facts: The parties descended from a common ancestor and the Settlement Officer found that the family remained joint and that no partition had occurred.

The Settlement Officer relied on historical property documents and accounts, acquisitions in the names of family members including minors, a family business arrangement, a family member’s payment connected with acquiring land rights, and evidence of shared possession and other family activities.

The disputed holdings were recorded in the names of members of different branches of the family, and the High Court noted the absence of evidence that the objecting family members had made individual acquisitions.
The Court accepted that the tenancy rights devolved under the applicable tenancy legislation, while the descendants continued as a joint Hindu family.
issues.conclusion: The holdings were held collectively by the members of the joint family for their benefit, and the recorded holders were not to be treated as holding them exclusively for themselves.
issues.legal_principle: Tenancy rights created by special legislation devolve under the provisions of the governing tenancy legislation. A joint Hindu family is not itself a juristic person capable of owning property independently; its members collectively own coparcenary property, each having an undivided interest until partition. The Court approved the proposition in Chotey Lal v. Jhandey Lal that members of a joint Hindu family together may be tenants of a holding and collectively own the property. The Court applied this principle to holdings recorded in individual family members’ names where the evidence supported joint family ownership.

rule.if: consolidation_property_dispute and family_continued_jointly and evidence_supports_joint_family_ownership and holdings_recorded_in_family_members_names and no_evidence_of_individual_acquisition

predicates.consolidation_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether land recorded in particular names is held for a family or by the recorded holders alone.
predicates.family_continued_jointly: The family remained undivided after the tenancy rights devolved to its members.
predicates.evidence_supports_joint_family_ownership: Documents, accounts, conduct, possession, or other evidence supports the finding that the property was acquired or held for the family.
predicates.holdings_recorded_in_family_members_name: The land is recorded in the names of individual members of different family branches rather than in the name of the family as an entity.
predicates.no_evidence_of_individual_acquisition: The record contains no evidence that the relevant family members acquired the disputed land individually for themselves.

issues.definition: Where an undivided family’s members are named in the land records and the evidence supports family ownership without showing individual acquisition, the members collectively hold the property for their benefit.

issues.legal_issue: A legal ground first raised before the Supreme Court, after not being raised before the earlier authorities or the High Court, may be declined for consideration.
material_facts: The appellants relied before the Supreme Court on provisions concerning declarations for unrecorded co-tenants and argued that the respondents could not claim shares without obtaining such a declaration.
The appellants had not raised those statutory arguments before the consolidation authorities or the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to consider the newly raised statutory arguments.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on the procedural posture of the case: the arguments under the cited tenancy-acquisition provisions had not been urged before any earlier authority or the High Court, and the Court was therefore not inclined to deal with them. No earlier case was cited for this conclusion.

predicates.final_appeal_proceeding: The matter is before the Supreme Court in an appeal after decisions by lower authorities and a reviewing court.
predicates.legal_ground_not_raised_before_lower_aut: A party raises a legal ground in the final appeal that it did not raise before the earlier authorities or the reviewing court.

issues.definition: When a legal ground is first raised in a final appeal after being omitted below, the court may decline to consider it.
